Cationic polymerization is a type of chain-growth polymerization that is initiated by a cationic species. The reactivity of monomers in cationic polymerization depends on their ability to stabilize a positive charge. Electron-donating groups increase the reactivity by stabilizing the carbocation formed during polymerization. 

2-Methoxypropene, with a methoxy group, is likely very reactive due to the strong electron-donating nature of the methoxy group. 4-Methoxyphenylacetylene is also quite reactive due to the methoxy group on the phenyl ring, but less so than 2-methoxypropene because the positive charge is not directly on the carbon next to the methoxy group. Phenylacetylene is less reactive than 4-methoxyphenylacetylene because it lacks the electron-donating methoxy group. 2-Methyl-2-butene is less reactive because it only has a methyl group as an electron donor. Lastly, 1,4-pentadiene is the least reactive since it lacks strong electron-donating groups.

Based on this reasoning, the correct order of reactivity from most to least should be:
2-methoxypropene > 4-methoxyphenylacetylene > phenylacetylene > 2-methyl-2-butene > 1,4-pentadiene.
